Record browser

Faceted, client-side browser over all protein-trait records — search by label, identifier, or definition; filter by axis, category, and source. Each record shows semantically related traits from a local text-embedding model.

Three 2-D maps sit alongside it: the corpus map projects a retained subset of record text embeddings (full-record or definition-only), the protein map lays out 68,657 Swiss-Prot proteins by the traits they carry, coloured by domain of life, and the sequence map lays out the canonical-example proteins by their ESM-2 protein-language-model embedding — sequence only, no annotation in the input — coloured by domain of life and filterable by sequence length and, for the half of them that carry one, by CATH class.

headings: How do individual residues change transport?
Reduced cell-surface availability is a supported explanation for the R252H taurocholate-uptake defect in the tested cells.
S267F changes NTCP transport in a substrate-dependent way, not simply by eliminating all transporter activity or surface abundance.
The 2015 taurocholate uptake result is explained by loss of NTCP sodium-contacting side-chain residue identities in SLC10A4.
Differences at mapped NTCP sites are sufficient to explain an absence of NTCP-like bile-acid transport by human SLC10A7.
Detectable preS1 binding alone establishes productive viral infection in the tested system.
2. Apo predictions are a separate comparison
Human NTCP E257 and Q261 participate in distinct sodium sites
Two modeled bile-salt molecules bind within the NTCP tunnel
NTCP TM4 residues interact with the bulevirtide myristoyl group
NTCP R252H links deficient surface availability to reduced uptake
NTCP S267F has opposite effects on two assayed substrates
5. Residue chemistry, local context and measured outcomes
Reuse an explanation without losing its limits
